results.corrected_claim: The skill really does say this. SKILL.md:88 (golden rule 5), checklists/pre-ship-checklist.md:9, references/02-hig-principles.md:162 and anti-pattern #2 in references/07-anti-patterns.md all ban Material in iOS 26+, and Apple says otherwise. HIG Materials, verbatim: "Don't use Liquid Glass in the content layer." ... "Instead, use standard materials for elements in the content layer, such as app backgrounds." Also: "In addition to Liquid Glass, iOS and iPadOS continue to provide four standard materials — ultra-thin, thin, regular (default), and thick — which you can use in the content layer to help create visual distinction." On legibility: "Help ensure legibility by using vibrant colors on top of materials" and "In general, avoid using quaternary on top of the thin and ultraThin materials, because the contrast is too low." SwiftUI `struct Material` is not deprecated. It is available on iOS 15.0+, iPadOS 15.0+, Mac Catalyst 15.0+, macOS 12.0+, tvOS 15.0+, visionOS 1.0+ and watchOS 8.0+, and every platform entry is deprecated:false. Its members are ultraThin, thin, regular, thick, ultraThick and bar. The correct rule: use Liquid Glass for the controls and navigation layer, and use standard materials (not glass) in the content layer. What Apple does ask you to remove is custom backgrounds and visual effect views on system bars, sheets and popovers (Adopting Liquid Glass: "Reduce your use of custom backgrounds" and "Audit the backgrounds of sheets and popovers").
results.notes: Sources read: HIG JSON at tutorials/data/design/human-interface-guidelines/materials.json and doc JSON swiftui/material.json (apple-doc). The newest HIG Materials change-log entry is September 9, 2025 ("Updated guidance for Liquid Glass"); there is no 2026 change. The skill makes the problem worse in anti-pattern #2, which replaces a material-backed "Header" Text with .glassEffect() and so puts glass into the content layer, which the HIG forbids. The skill also contradicts itself: references/06-performance.md:74 says .regularMaterial "is still legal for full backgrounds".

results.corrected_claim: The skill lines exist as described. references/05-accessibility.md:73 recommends a `Color.black.opacity(0.15).blendMode(.plusDarker)` scrim, and line 74 calls switching to .regular a "last resort". references/06-performance.md:61 recommends "Use `.clear` variant (lighter)" as a performance fix; line 186 and pre-ship-checklist.md:64 also tie video playback to .clear. Apple says the following. HIG Materials: "Only use clear Liquid Glass for components that appear over visually rich backgrounds." On regular: "Use the regular variant when background content might create legibility issues, or when components have a significant amount of text, such as alerts, sidebars, or popovers." On clear: "Use this variant for components that float above media backgrounds — such as photos and videos". On dimming: "If the underlying content is bright, consider adding a dark dimming layer of 35% opacity" and "If the underlying content is sufficiently dark, or if you use standard media playback controls from AVKit that provide their own dimming layer, you don't need to apply a dimming layer." The Glass.clear doc gives the declaration `static var clear: Glass { get }`, available on iOS 26.0+, iPadOS 26.0+, Mac Catalyst 26.0+, macOS 26.0+, tvOS 26.0+ and watchOS 26.0+ (visionOS is not listed). It says: "When using clear glass, ensure content remains legible by adding a dimming layer or other treatment beneath the glass." Its example is `.glassEffect(.clear).background(.black.opacity(0.3))`. WWDC25 session 219 says: "They should never be mixed". Clear is only for when "the element you're applying it to is over media-rich content", "your content layer won't be negatively affected by introducing a dimming layer", and "the content sitting above it is bold and bright." No Apple source says .clear costs less to render. Apple's performance advice is to use GlassEffectContainer and limit the number of glass effects on screen.
results.notes: Also checked: swiftui/glass/clear.json (apple-doc), the WWDC25 219 transcript (apple-video), and swiftui/applying-liquid-glass-to-custom-views.json, which never mentions clear or any performance difference. One small overstatement in the finding: the skill does have a one-line usage hint for clear (01-api-reference.md:81 "Over photos, video, vivid imagery" and 03-design-tokens.md:93). What it lacks is the dimming requirement, the never-mix rule and the three-condition test. Its 15% scrim with .plusDarker is weaker than Apple's documented 30–35% dimming, and Apple never uses that blend mode.

results.corrected_claim: All the quotes check out. HIG Branding (change log: "September 9, 2026 — Refined guidance for using brand color."): "Apply your app's accent color judiciously." "Using your brand color too broadly can overwhelm your interface and dilute its impact. Minimize its use on controls and instead use it intentionally for primary actions or status indicators, like badges for unread content or an icon for the selected tab in a tab bar. To express your brand through color, consider moving it into the content layer, where it scrolls beneath Liquid Glass controls and gets picked up dynamically." HIG Color (alert-date December 16, 2025): "Apply color sparingly to the Liquid Glass material, and to symbols or text on the material." "If you apply color, reserve it for elements that truly benefit from emphasis, such as status indicators or primary actions." "To emphasize primary actions, apply color to the background rather than to symbols or text." "Refrain from adding color to the background of multiple controls." "If your app features colorful backgrounds or visually rich content, prefer a monochromatic appearance for toolbars and tab bars, or choose an accent color with sufficient visual differentiation." "...in apps with primarily monochromatic content or backgrounds, choosing your brand color as the app accent color can be an effective way...". WWDC26 session 251, "Communicate your brand identity on iOS": "our recommendation is to move color into the content area of your app, into the scroll view. That way, Liquid Glass controls sit above the content layer and pick up your brand color dynamically." This shows the skill's rule "For brand color, tint the content (icon, label), not the glass" is wrong. In Apple's guidance, brand color belongs in the scrolling content layer, not on control icons or labels, and tint on controls is kept for one primary action (on its background) and for status indicators. A red/green/orange semantic tint table applied across many glass controls goes against "Refrain from adding color to the background of multiple controls."
results.notes: Sources read: HIG branding.json and color.json (apple-other / HIG) and the WWDC26 251 video page transcript (apple-video). The skill's canonical primary CTA (.glassProminent with the tint on the background) matches HIG Color, so it can stay. The problem is the brand-color rule (02-hig-principles.md:103, 03-design-tokens.md:67, checklist:34) and the semantic tint table at 02-hig-principles.md:93-99.

results.corrected_claim: The example matches the description: examples/09-HealthTodayScreen.swift:109-110 applies `.badge(3).tint(.red)` to a topBarTrailing toolbar Button, and line 112 adds `ToolbarSpacer(.fixed, placement: .topBarTrailing)`. HIG Toolbars (alert-date December 16, 2025), verbatim: "Reduce the use of toolbar backgrounds and tinted controls. Any custom backgrounds and appearances you use might overlay or interfere with background effects that the system provides." "Use the .prominent style for key actions such as Done or Submit. This separates and tints the action so there's a clear focal point. Only specify one primary action, and put it on the trailing side of the toolbar." "Prefer system-provided symbols without borders. System-provided symbols are familiar, automatically receive appropriate coloring and vibrancy...". Badges are supported: the View.badge(_:) doc says "Badges appear in list rows, tab bars, toolbar items, and menus." HIG Branding and Color endorse badges as status indicators. So keep `.badge(3)` and drop `.tint(.red)`.
results.notes: The HIG Toolbars page itself never mentions badges. The badge endorsement comes from HIG Branding ("status indicators, like badges for unread content") and HIG Color. On the fixed spacer, this finding's evidence says nothing; see finding 18. In short, Apple documents ToolbarSpacer(.fixed) as the way to split items that share one glass background, which is exactly what line 112 does. Apple's 2026 guidance (iPhone Duo HIG, the tech talk, and "Audit toolbar customizations") now discourages manual fixed spacing and prefers ToolbarItemGroup, so removing it is a recommendation rather than the fix of a clear error. Also relevant to this example: HIG Toolbars says bordered or circled symbols are unnecessary, and the profile button uses "person.crop.circle.fill".

results.corrected_claim: The quotes are verbatim. Adopting Liquid Glass: "Audit toolbar customizations. Review anything custom you do to display items in your toolbars, like your use of fixed spacers or custom items, as these can appear inconsistent with system behavior." HIG Designing for iPhone Duo (new page, September 9, 2026): "Group related toolbar items instead of spacing them manually. Groups you create with ToolbarItemGroup (SwiftUI) or UIBarButtonItemGroup (UIKit) provide space between items and other groups automatically, and adapt as the available space changes, so avoid adding fixed spacing yourself." Tech talk "Raise the bar with iPhone Duo" (tech-talks/111462): "By default, flexible spacers are zero size in the vertical axis. But fixed spacers continue to respect their minimum size. Your app shouldn't be creating additional spacing, regardless of if a bar is horizontal or vertical." Two things are wrong or missing in the finding. (1) The same Adopting Liquid Glass article says "You can create a fixed spacer to separate items that share a background using these APIs:" and lists SpacerSizing.fixed and ToolbarSpacer, so Apple still documents fixed spacers for splitting a shared glass background. (2) HIG Toolbars does not limit fixed space to text-labeled buttons. Besides "Keep actions with text labels separate ... Add separation by inserting fixed space between the buttons", it also says "To position items in the groupings you want, pin them to the leading edge, center, or trailing edge, and insert space between buttons or other items where appropriate." The ToolbarSpacer doc reads: "A standard space item in toolbars." "A space item creates visual breaks in the toolbar between items. Spacers can have a standard fixed size or be flexible and push items apart." It is available on iOS 26.0, iPadOS 26.0, Mac Catalyst 26.0 and macOS 26.0, with init(_:placement:) taking a SpacerSizing. Correct guidance for the skill: describe ToolbarSpacer(.fixed) as the way to split items that would otherwise share one glass background, not as "breathing room". Prefer ToolbarItemGroup groupings, audit any fixed spacers, and avoid manual fixed spacing because fixed spacers keep their size on iPhone Duo's vertical bars.
results.notes: Sources read: HIG designing-for-iphone-duo.json, toolbars.json (HIG), technologyoverviews/adopting-liquid-glass.json and swiftui/toolbarspacer.json (apple-doc), and the tech-talks/111462 transcript (apple-video). In the tech talk, "additional spacing" follows directly after the spacer sentences, but the talk never defines its scope. The SwiftUI updates page for June and September 2026 has no ToolbarSpacer change or deprecation. The verdict is partial because the claim "HIG Toolbars still recommends fixed space only between adjacent text-labeled buttons" is wrong ("only"), and because the finding leaves out Apple's explicit endorsement of fixed spacers for separating items that share a background.

results.corrected_claim:
The skill really has no mention of scroll edge effects. Grep finds no ScrollEdgeEffectStyle, scrollEdgeEffectStyle(_:for:), scrollEdgeEffectHidden or safeAreaBar; the skill uses safeAreaInset for floating bars (patterns/glass-floating-toolbar.md and examples 05, 06, 08). Verified sources:
- HIG Scroll views (change log "June 8, 2026 — Updated guidance for scroll edge effects."): "Prefer the automatic scroll edge effect style. Where possible, use the default automatic style ... This style provides a more opaque visual separation for top toolbars that contain a large number of controls, text that appears outside of Liquid Glass controls, and pinned table headers. If you use the soft scroll edge effect style instead, thoroughly test your interface..." Also: "Only use a scroll edge effect when a scroll view is behind floating interface elements." and "Apply one scroll edge effect per view."
- WWDC26 session 278, "Modernize your UIKit app": "the .automatic style no longer switches between the existing soft and hard styles but provides its own visuals for additional clarity. If you have overridden the style from .automatic previously, that decision should be re-evaluated, especially when set to .soft, as that no longer matches the default system appearance."
- Platforms State of the Union (session 102): "When content scrolls under floating bars, a uniform toolbar appears across the top and keeps the text legible while improving contrast. This effect is applied automatically for standard toolbars and can be customized using the existing scroll edge effect APIs."
- WWDC26 session 289, "Modernize your AppKit app": "The automatic NSScrollEdgeEffectStyle resolves to a hard-edge effect, when there is free-floating text, like the window title in the title bar."
- HIG Layout (updated September 9, 2026): "Instead of applying a solid or semi-opaque background color beneath controls, use a scroll edge effect to visually elevate controls above content."
- iOS & iPadOS 27 release notes, UIKit New Features: "The container view of a UIScrollEdgeElementContainerInteraction may contribute its size and position to the overall shape of the scroll edge effect. (179191941) (FB23027596)".
Declarations: `struct ScrollEdgeEffectStyle` with `static var automatic: ScrollEdgeEffectStyle`, `static var hard: ScrollEdgeEffectStyle` and `static var soft: ScrollEdgeEffectStyle`, available from 26.0 on iOS, iPadOS, Mac Catalyst, macOS, tvOS, visionOS and watchOS. `nonisolated func scrollEdgeEffectStyle(_ style: ScrollEdgeEffectStyle?, for edges: Edge.Set) -> some View` is 26.0. `safeAreaBar(edge:alignment:spacing:content:)` is 26.0, and Apple says it "extends the edge effect of any scroll views affected by the inset safe area".
results.notes:
Caveats on scope:
- The State of the Union passage sits among macOS and iPad statements ("every window on macOS ...", followed by "both on macOS and iPadOS"), and its platform is never stated. Do not present it as iOS-specific.
- Session 289 is about macOS and AppKit only.
- The UIScrollEdgeElementContainerInteraction item is UIKit only. The class itself is iOS 26.0+; only the shape-contribution behavior is a 27 release note.
- The iOS 27 change to automatic visuals is stated in the UIKit session 278. The SwiftUI updates page for 2026 has no scroll-edge entries, and the ScrollEdgeEffectStyle doc still describes automatic as choosing by platform and context.
The HIG Toolbars page also tells you to "use a ScrollEdgeEffectStyle when necessary to distinguish the toolbar area from the content area".
